#4961. Bitcoin’s $60,000 bear market is testing miners harder than the 2022 crypto winter

Bitcoin’s hashrate rebounds as mining revenue per unit hits $29.36 and AI competes for power and infrastructure.

Bitcoin’s hashrate rebounded above 1,000 exahashes per second in the week to Nov. 23, while the expected dollar revenue per unit of that computing power fell over the same week.

Luxor’s weekly mining update put the seven-day average hashrate at 1,033 EH/s, up 7.8% from 959 EH/s a week earlier.

Over the same week, dollar hashprice fell 3%, from $30.27 to $29.36 per petahash per second per day. Hashprice is the gross daily revenue a miner can expect from a fixed amount of computing power, before electricity and other costs.

The rebound came with Bitcoin trading near $60,000 on Nov. 24, about 52.5% below its October 2025 price record. The 30-day average hashrate was about 1,013 EH/s on Nov. 23, or 91.2% of the roughly 1,110 EH/s high recorded on Nov. 11, 2025, in the period analyzed.

The average had fallen to 896 EH/s on July 28, about 19.3% below that high.

The same point in the two previous Bitcoin bear markets gives that 91% some context.

The comparison uses the 30-day average 413 days after each cycle’s peak daily price close, measured against the highest 30-day hashrate recorded between the price peak and day 413.

It also uses Blockchain.com’s daily estimates, with Coin Metrics readings filling three missing dates in November 2025. A 30-day average smooths swings when blocks arrive more quickly or slowly by chance.

In the 2017–18 cycle, mining power kept rising after the December 2017 price peak. It reached 52.4 EH/s in October 2018, then fell to 37.6 EH/s on Dec. 25. By Feb. 2, 2019, the matched date, it had recovered to 41.9 EH/s, just under 80% of its high.

In the 2021–22 cycle, hashrate also set a high well after the price peak, reaching 265.2 EH/s in November 2022. It stood at 246.8 EH/s on Dec. 26, 2022, or 93.1% of its high. Today’s network is slightly farther below its peak than it was at that point in 2022 and closer than it was after the 2018 slump.

Bitcoin’s 30-day network hashrate as a share of its cycle high, measured 413 days after each peak daily price close. Each high is the strongest 30-day estimate from the price peak through the comparison date.

Source: Blockchain.com 2017–19 · · Blockchain.com 2020–22 · · Blockchain.com 2024–26 · · Coin Metrics, November 2025 · · Galaxy Research, price peaks · · Blockchain.com, methodology

Hashrate Index recorded a 2022 hashprice low of $55.94 per petahash per second per day, almost twice its Nov. 23 reading. The April 2024 halving cut Bitcoin’s fixed subsidy from 6.25 to 3.125 BTC per block. Transaction fees add to that subsidy, but they made up just 0.64% of block rewards in Luxor’s latest weekly snapshot.

Bitcoin’s mining difficulty fell 9.13% on Nov. 14. Using power prices and machine economics, Luxor’s West Texas analysis estimated that miners cutting electricity use there could account for roughly three-quarters of the 91 EH/s drop in the network’s 14-day average around that adjustment.

Riot Platforms previously earned credits for reducing power use.

Core Scientific’s third-quarter results show $215.4 million in quarterly colocation revenue, and the company was billing for 485 megawatts of capacity as of Sept. 30.

IREN said its Horizon 1 facility entered service for Microsoft during the September quarter. The company’s mining revenue fell to $28 million from $67 million in the previous quarter.

Riot’s November results show the company mined 1,637 BTC in the third quarter, up from 1,406 a year earlier, and separately disclosed a 910-megawatt powered-land lease for AI at Corsicana with the first delivery scheduled for September 2027.

A sustained loss of mining power would lengthen the expected time between blocks at the prevailing difficulty.

Bitcoin adjusts the difficulty every 2,016 blocks to bring the pace back toward one block every 10 minutes.

#4960. U.S DOJ seeks to seize $1.1 billion in crypto linked to North Korea’s Binance hack

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

The U.S Department of Justice (DOJ) has taken legal action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptos stolen from Binance on 29th October 2026. With this move, the government has now moved beyond simply freezing the stolen funds and is now seeking their legal forfeiture.

According to the DOJ, the stolen funds had already been placed under a restraining order, which was the reason why they were prevented from being transferred or accessed while authorities pursued recovery efforts.

Remarking on the same, Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said,

The Department of Justice has long prioritized victims and their rights, and the commencement of this forfeiture action so soon after the restraint of these same assets reflects our commitment to ensuring that victims remain at the forefront of our work.

Binance suffered a cryptocurrency theft worth more than $6.3 billion, which the U.S authorities linked to North Korean cyber hackers.

Following the attack, the hackers allegedly used sophisticated laundering techniques to move the stolen cryptocurrency across different wallets and potentially convert it.

However, the FBI, U.S Secret Service, and the IRS has worked alongside private-sector companies to track the transactions and identify wallets holding the stolen funds.

As its stands, the U.S. government has frozen and seized nearly $3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from multiple sources since the Binance theft. The latest $1.1 billion forfeiture action is part of this broader recovery effort and does not represent an additional $1.1 billion on top of the nearly $3 billion already recovered or restrained.

If this forfeiture is successful, the action could help return the recovered assets to their rightful owners.

#4958. LINK, AAVE and UNI Now Supported by Fidelity

Fidelity Investments now supports three new cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

The firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Fidelity's three new listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where users can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where users can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

On July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the company introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it launched Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible users can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

#4957. How to Launch a Fintech Product Without Building Infrastructure From Scratch

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Picture a payments product built around one promise: a small business pays an overseas contractor without juggling several banking portals. The transfer screen is the easy part. Behind it sit customer verification, a ledger, payment connections and a way to trace a transfer that fails. Each is a separate engineering project, and none is the reason customers choose the product. Using existing infrastructure for the standard parts is the shortest route to launch, provided the team knows which parts are standard.

Before it accepts a first customer, a contractor-payment service needs identity and business verification (KYC and KYB checks), a reliable record of balances and transactions, connections to payment networks, transaction monitoring, and back-office tools for investigating problems.

The accounting component is called a ledger. It records movements and obligations inside the product; it does not send money through a banking network. That takes financial partners and technical integrations. A transfer that has been submitted has not necessarily settled, so the application has to track and display statuses accurately.

Cards and crypto add their own layers. Cards add an issuing partner and a card processor. Crypto payments need wallet technology, transaction screening, and connections to custody or liquidity services. The exact combination depends on the business model and the markets it serves.

Customers of a contractor-payment service typically care about clear fees, reliable payment tracking, and the ability to manage recipients in several countries. Those are where the product wins or loses. A homemade document-verification system is not: customers will never compare you on it.

So the company can integrate identity checks, use a ready-made ledger and connect to an existing payment provider, while it designs the customer journey, sets prices and runs the product. Buying software does not transfer every business or regulatory obligation to the supplier. Those depend on the services involved, local rules and contracts with financial partners.

That is the logic behind launching a fintech product without building infrastructure from scratch: skip the engineering that does not differentiate you, keep the decisions that do.

The build vs buy decision for a fintech platform involves more than the initial price: maintenance and technical control weigh just as much.

An in-house system gives engineers direct control over code and architecture. They can implement unusual transaction rules without waiting for a vendor, which can justify the investment when a product’s financial logic is genuinely distinctive.

The team also owns maintenance, testing, security updates and every change to external integrations. If a banking partner changes its API, someone has to update the connection without interrupting live operations. The ability to write the software is only part of the cost of owning it.

Existing infrastructure moves part of that load to a supplier. An established ledger, onboarding workflow or administration tool saves the team from building a standard function from scratch. The buyer still configures it, connects it to other systems and tests the complete transaction flow.

Neither route has a guaranteed price advantage. Platform fees, integration charges, internal engineering time, future changes and the cost of switching suppliers all belong in the comparison. A sensible split is often to build the customer-facing logic, buy the ledger and keep direct relationships with financial partners.

Speed comes from two places: less code to write, and more work running in parallel. While engineers configure a platform, the business can negotiate with banking and card partners and prepare its compliance work. When everything is built in-house, partner integration and testing have to wait for the software.

An API lets two applications exchange requests and data, for example to submit a verification request or ask a partner to start a transfer. Developers do not recreate the provider’s service, though they still handle timeouts, errors and unexpected responses.

Modular fintech infrastructure supplies several components designed to work together. A company can start with accounts, onboarding and transaction records, then add cards later, so each new function does not begin as a separate development project. The card program itself still needs its financial arrangements.

White-label software can supply the web or mobile interface too, covering routine screens for registration, balances and transaction history. Whether the services behind those screens are available in the company’s chosen market is a separate question.

Crypto follows the same logic. A fiat and crypto fintech platform keeps conventional accounts and digital-asset flows in one system. Crypto processing software typically handles the payment side: accepting and tracking incoming transactions, wallet and address management, monitoring and reporting. Custody, exchange and settlement usually come from separate providers. When evaluating white-label crypto processing software, ask which of these functions are built in, which are integrations, and which you will have to arrange yourself.

A feature list does not show readiness for launch. A provider may support transfers, wallets and cards, but each function has to be available for your target countries, currencies, customers and partners. A demo helps only if the proposed configuration can be deployed.

Then ask about daily operations. Who investigates a failed transfer? Can the team access transaction histories and reconcile them against external records? Who maintains integrations when partners change their technical requirements? What data can be exported if you move to another platform?

Keep configuration separate from external dependencies when judging any promised launch date. Contracts, financial partnerships, compliance decisions and testing sit outside the software.

FinHarbor is a financial infrastructure software platform for launching neobanks, wallets, payment services and crypto-enabled products. It covers onboarding with configurable KYC/KYB tiers, accounts and transactions, an admin panel for fees, limits and roles, and white-label web and mobile apps. Every function is available through an API, and the platform integrates with payment systems, banking rails, card issuers, crypto gateways and KYC providers. It supports fiat, crypto and hybrid models.

FinHarbor is a software provider, not a bank: the licence stays with the client or its regulated partner. In a launch plan it replaces the build of standard components, while partner contracts, licensing and compliance decisions, and testing still run in parallel.

A practical next step is to map your product’s components against the list above and see which ones a platform already covers.

#4955. Bitcoin faces a familiar macro threat as the US prepares another round of tariffs

A reported US tariff push targeting 16 economies could reignite trade tensions and expose Bitcoin to renewed market volatility.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Nov. 24 that the US was preparing higher tariffs on China, the European Union, and other trading partners, which could impact Bitcoin.

Citing people familiar with the plans, the Journal reported that US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer could release the findings of a months-long investigation into manufacturing overcapacity as soon as this week.

On Nov. 24, the USTR docket still showed the investigation opened in March and four days of hearings in May, listing no determination or tariff schedule for the case. A check of published USTR notices in the Federal Register found none dated Nov. 19 through Nov. 24.

The available White House, Treasury, and Commerce trade agency listings carried no announcement of the action described in the report. Importers still have no published list of the goods that would face these duties, the rates that would apply or the date they would start.

On Nov. 20, Greer told Bloomberg Television he expected the work to be finished by year-end. He declined to specify which economies might face additional tariffs.

USTR opened the investigations on March 11 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and is examining whether policies such as subsidies sustain more manufacturing capacity than demand supports and whether those practices burden or restrict US commerce.

The agency’s fact sheet described the sectors it wanted to examine. An investigation of how a product is made or subsidized leaves open which products, if any, may face duties.

The inquiry covers 16 economies, including the EU. The March 17 initiation notice also lists Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India. Hearings ran from May 5 through May 8.

Under Section 304 of the Trade Act, USTR must determine whether the practices are actionable. If it makes an affirmative finding, it must decide what action, if any, to take. The law requires the trade representative to publish the determination and the facts it rests on in the Federal Register.

Public hearings ended in May. The USTR docket still showed no determination on Nov. 24.

A USTR determination would establish whether the practices are actionable and, if so, what action USTR should take.

Scope is the public docket checked on Nov. 24, 2026. Marker spacing shows the order of events and does not measure elapsed time. No tariff outcome is assumed.

The dates come from USTR’s initiation release and case docket. The lower diagram shows the determination and publication requirements in Section 304 of the Trade Act.

On July 23, USTR announced final duties on 60 economies after separate investigations into their failures to impose and enforce bans on imports made with forced labor.

On April 9, 2025, President Donald Trump posted that he had authorized a 90-day pause in some higher tariffs while raising the rate for China.

The executive order dated the same day amended the tariff schedule and applied the changes to covered goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, at or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern daylight time on April 10.

The reciprocal tariff changes came under different authority from the current investigation.

The written terms tell the company whether its goods fall under the amended tariff schedule and whether its shipment enters before or after the cutoff. The applicable rate can depend on those details and on whether an exemption applies.

After Trump signaled a possible tariff increase on China in October 2025, Bitcoin fell during a broader selloff. That episode shows why a tariff headline can impact crypto investors before importers have any new duties to enter on customs paperwork.

If the USTR determination leads to tariffs, the product coverage, rates, and entry dates will show where costs change and when. Until USTR publishes its findings, the docket remains the place to look for the public decision.

#4952. End of Crypto Trading? How AI Replaces Ones Who Pumped Bitcoin (BTC)

The “pump” trade could be taken to new extremes. While some may still be able to use their influence to promote a token, causing others to pile in, it could now be left up to AI to scour socials/wallet activity for abnormal trading volume, assess momentum rankings, etc. and execute on these opportunities faster than those that may be slower to react.

All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing issues with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.

Automation is not necessarily a new occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.

A February 2026 study from the Journal of Futures Markets found sub-second trading patterns in BTC/ETH perpetual/spot markets exhibiting behavior consistent with algo trading for liquidity, increasing volatility and trading costs with no significant impact on prices.

In August 2026, Binance rolled out Agent OS allowing builders to access exchange trading functionality and data via AI agents.

Coinbase Ventures released a comprehensive breakdown of the crypto agentic stack from data, to agent building tools, to execution/compliance in November. Instead of dictating each trade, users may be able to assign high-level goals (i.e. follow momentum, hedge position, etc.) for agents to implement 24/7.

Automation will likely accelerate across the crypto space. While macro events, ETF inflows/outflows, large holders, etc. will still have an impact on Bitcoin, it’s likely that many more aspects/trades will become automated.

Time will tell how pervasive agentic trading will become, but the era of a small group of traders/influencers/chat rooms able to move the needle via FOMO/hype seems poised to face stiff competition from AI that never sleeps.

AI is not necessarily intelligent. A 2026 study published in the journal Frontiers in Blockchain studied machine-learning strategies using crypto market data and found that many strategies became highly overfit and offered no viable edge for retail traders once realistic trading fees were taken into account.

Also, strategies that performed well on one cryptocurrency did not necessarily perform well on others. Faster processing speeds can’t make bad data good, can’t identify all false narratives and can’t insulate a strategy from sudden shifts in market regimes.

Are institutional investors still relevant? Can they protect themselves? Absolutely.

Institutions are (and will continue to be) an important source of capital, liquidity and price discovery (particularly for Bitcoin). A 2026 study using BTC data from 2012–2025 found that as the market has matured, Bitcoin has seen increased trading volume, decreasing transaction costs and increasing market efficiency.

Wintermute reported that in the first half of 2026 institutional clients accounted for 72% of total spot trading volume on its OTC desk (note: this is Wintermute’s OTC desk and is not representative of the entire market). It’s also worth noting that many institutional investors do employ quantitative strategies and state-of-the-art execution technologies.

While larger investors may have access to better data, faster infrastructure, cross-venue surveillance capabilities and stricter risk management protocols (and can limit their exposure and monitor abnormal order flow), there’s only so much that institutional investors can do to protect themselves.

Institutional investors can’t control a 24/7 global market with liquidity spread across multiple venues and derivatives markets. They also can’t assume that all AIs are created equal/safe (as Binance’s launch of its own AI demonstrated prompt injection risks and limited visibility into external AIs’ trading logic/reasons for trading).

Finally, during times of stress, risk management/contingency protocols (used by many investors) could be a crowded exit for funds that employ similar strategies.

The future is not “AI replaces every trader.” It will likely see continued automation of certain aspects of trading (i.e. execution, short-term alpha hunting, etc.) and a continued shift in the value-add that humans bring to the table (i.e. capital allocation, risk management, original research, granting/trading bots permission to trade, etc.).

While AI/bots may continue to squeeze spreads in normal market conditions, they may exacerbate drawdowns/cascades during times of market stress as strategies compete with one another.

At the end of the day, Bitcoin will still be bought/sold, it’s just a question of who gets to make those decisions.

#4951. XRP’s shrinking exchange supply may be telling investors the wrong story

Uphold accounts for 82% of the weekly drop in tracked XRP exchange balances, with 270 million XRP sent to unlabeled wallets.

Wallets attributed to Uphold accounted for about 82% of the 545.3 million XRP decline in tracked exchange balances in the seven days to Nov. 24.

The weekly balance breakdown from XRP Insights compares the same addresses on Nov. 17 and Nov. 24. At the end of the week, the tracker counted about 1.25 billion XRP in 24 Uphold-attributed wallets.

Three payments from Uphold-labeled addresses sent about 270 million XRP to three unlabeled wallets on Nov. 23. At follow-up checks the next day, each still held roughly 90 million tokens.

The broader snapshot at 08:01 UTC on Nov. 24 put exchange-attributed holdings at 21.69 billion XRP across 708 addresses. The weekly calculation used the 707 wallets already tracked on Nov. 17.

Coinbase-attributed balances fell by 35.9 million XRP, and Bithumb’s fell by 24.7 million, while Binance-attributed wallets added about 181,000.

Nov. 17–24, 2026 comparison across the same 707 XRP Ledger wallets tracked by XRP Insights.

Uphold-attributed wallets accounted for about 82% of the net decline across the 24 tracked exchanges.

Public labels group XRP Ledger wallets by attributed exchange. The comparison uses the same addresses at both dates and includes custody balances. It measures a net change in those balances.

The Uphold share is 446,819,576.34 divided by 545,288,925.25 XRP. The other exchanges’ combined decline is the difference, 98,469,348.91 XRP. Bar lengths use the unrounded proportion. XRP amounts are rounded to one decimal million and the share to a whole percent.

Public labels group XRP Ledger wallets by attributed exchange. The comparison uses the same addresses at both dates and includes custody balances. It measures a net change in those balances.

Between 16:21:22 and 16:21:42 UTC on Nov. 23, the XRP Ledger recorded three successful payments from three separate addresses labeled Uphold by XRPSCAN.

The first payment, second payment, and third payment each delivered just over 90 million XRP. Each sending address was left with 1 token, and each receiving address held about 40 tokens before the transfers.

The account histories for rhDoUm, rP2Sxx and rKB4EP show one subsequent incoming payment of 0.000010 XRP to each wallet. No outgoing transaction appeared by the time XRPSCAN balances were checked between 13:12 and 13:13 UTC on Nov. 24.

On Nov. 20, one unlabeled address sent 50 XRP to each of the three. Later that day, each sent 10 tokens to the same Uphold-labeled address.

Those payments establish a connection among the addresses, but Uphold’s public transparency report names none of the three recipients.

XRPSONAR’s Nov. 23 flow series counted 271.6 million XRP sent from its known Uphold wallets and 2.4 million received, leaving a net outflow of 269.2 million tokens that day.

The same series showed a separate 178.7 million XRP net outflow on Nov. 20.

In October, XRP Insights attributed most of an earlier monthly decline to Uphold moving tokens into newly used wallets outside the tracked set. The labeled balance can fall even when the exchange still controls the coins.

A useful test would compare how much was offered within the same distance of the market midpoint on the same spot pairs and venues at comparable times before and after Nov. 23.

Measuring buy orders over the same price range would show how much a seller could trade near the quoted price.

Repeated readings would show whether any difference in quoted depth persisted beyond a single snapshot. A thinner set of sell orders in that range would show that buyers could get less XRP close to the prevailing quote on those markets.

#4950. Signal Calls OS-Level AI an 'Existential Threat' and Blocks Screenshots to Fight It

Signal Calls OS-Level AI an 'Existential Threat' and Blocks Screenshots to Fight It

Signal is moving to wall off its messages from the AI assistants now baked into smartphones, restricting screenshots so that systems like Google’s Gemini and Apple’s Siri can’t quietly scan and store users’ private conversations.

The encrypted-messaging nonprofit said Thursday it will block the latest agentic AI features built into iOS 27 and, on Android, automatically enable a “screen security” setting whenever it detects an AI assistant trying to read a user’s Signal screen.

The move extends a tactic Signal first used last year against Microsoft’s Recall, the Windows feature that captured periodic screenshots; the company blocked it to keep Recall from storing images of Signal messages by default.

The concern, Signal says, is that operating-system AI agents work by “scanning” whatever is on a user’s screen, which means Signal data gets captured and handed to those systems to process.

Once that happens, the content lands in whatever local database or remote server the AI is using, outside Signal’s control and beyond the encryption guarantees that have defined the app for a decade.

Users who still want to take screenshots can disable the protection in Signal’s settings, though the company warns that doing so could expose their messages, and their contacts’ messages, to the AI agents.

Signal also conceded the fix is incomplete: It doesn’t stop sneakier methods of access, such as pulling data straight from a device’s filesystem, and it can’t yet be implemented on macOS, where Signal says Apple lacks the documented tools to block screenshots reliably.

Signal also flagged third-party agents like Meta’s Muse, warning they exploit accessibility permissions meant to help people, not to serve as “a skeleton key” for AI.

The worry isn’t hypothetical: A journalist found that Muse had accessed his private iMessages despite his settings and then gave a false explanation of how it knew their contents, an episode that crystallized fears about how much agents can reach once granted deep device permissions.

Signal’s move lands amid a broader reckoning over AI agents accessing data they shouldn’t, from rogue agents breaching systems to banks scrambling to keep autonomous software out of sensitive accounts.

#4949. Can BNB defend its crucial $500 weekly swing low before 2026 ends?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Binance Coin [BNB] presented an attractive trading opportunity. The crypto market, for the most part, has a strongly bearish bias.

The selling pressure that drove the two giants, Bitcoin [BTC] and Ethereum [ETH], below key psychological levels such as $60k and $2,000, had a considerable impact across the altcoin market as well.

Monday, the 23rd of November, saw heightened volatility and triggered $520.89 million in short liquidations alone across the crypto sphere, according to CoinGlass data.

It will come as no surprise, then, that the Binance Coin trade setup was also a bearish one.

The bearish price action that began in October-November 2025 eventually drove BNB back to the $500 lows. The last time BNB had been so close to this key support was in early 2025.

Yet, it could be revisited before 2026 comes to an end.

A bullish internal structure break (green) was seen, but the bearish imbalances put a halt to this rally. The imbalances BNB left behind during its descent from $933 to $570 in January-February 2026 acted as a supply zone.

Combined with Bitcoin and Ethereum weakness, the crypto markets stalled, helping establish a BNB correction back to the $537 swing low and potentially toward $500.

Technically, the swing structure was bullish and will remain so until a weekly BNB close below $500.

Zooming in, we find a bearish BNB structure. The fair value gap (red box) from $551.45-$576.39 was swept, helped by Monday’s volatility. Failure to break beyond $600 cemented the bears’ dominance.

It also established the next target- $503.75. On the way, the $530 zone, which had served as a local support in recent days, could temporarily stall the sellers.

The 1-hour chart aligned with the higher timeframes. A session close below $550.82 on this timeframe confirmed a bearish structure shift, and a retest of the $555 supply zone, another imbalance on this timeframe, and the subsequent rejection strongly signaled further downside.

An hourly session close above $562.19 would invalidate this sell setup, while the $503 and $500 remain feasible targets.
